newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech PM sees house compromise on German WW2 pact.
newsitem.headline: Czech PM sees house compromise on German WW2 pact.

text.p: Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus said on Monday he was hopeful for a compromise on a resolution to be debated in parliament alongside a post-World War Two reconciliation pact with Germany, the CTK news agency reported.

"The text of this resolution I see as hopeful, and I hope it will be possible to find such (an acceptable) formulation," it quoted Klaus as saying after a one-hour meeting with parliamentary chairman and opposition leader Milos Zeman.
Klaus and Zeman declined to reveal any of the wording of the compromise text of the new resolution, CTK said.

The Czech-German declaration, which tries to put an official political end to animosities between the neighbours stemming from World War Two and its aftermath, was signed by Klaus and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl last month.
Although it does not require parliamentary approval, the declaration received support from a large majority voting in the German parliament on January 30.

But the bilateral pact, which apologises for Nazi attrocities during the 1938-45 occupation of Czech territory and for the brutality of Czech post-War expulsions of ethnic Germans, faces a rougher road in the Czech parliament.

Zeman, whose opposition Social Democratic party has waivered on its support for the declaration, has been pushing for a separate resolution which would address concerns and permit the house's approval of the bilateral document.

Zeman, among other concerns, has sought a reference to the agreement drawn up by the victorious allies at the 1945 Potsdam conference, which Czechs believe formed an internationally legal basis for the expulsion of ethnic Germans.

However, in the bilateral declaration, the Czechs do not apologise for the expulsion of the estimated 2.5 million ethnic Germans after the war, but rather for the "excessive brutality" used in carrying out the expulsions.
